topic: TradingView Pine Script vs Python - which to learn first

article.title: Write Pine Script First. Python Can Wait Ninety Days.
article.meta_description: Pine Script vs Python for traders: why I ship in Pine first, and the exact point where Python stops being optional. From a dev who trades full time.
article.author: Alex Turner
article.intro: Write Pine Script first. Move to Python the week Pine physically blocks something you need, and not a week earlier. I learned that the expensive way in March 2023, when I ported a working mean reversion script off TradingView into a Python backtester and spent eleven days on data plumbing, timezone bugs and a Parquet cache before I got a single equity curve out of it. The Pine version had taken about forty minutes. The Python version was better, eventually, but those eleven days bought me nothing a trader would care about.
article.intro2: The usual advice frames this as a language choice, which is why it's usually wrong. Pine Script and Python sit at different points on a curve of setup cost versus ceiling. Pine has almost no setup cost and a hard ceiling. Python has a brutal setup cost and effectively no ceiling. If you don't have a strategy yet, the setup cost is the only variable that matters, because the thing that kills new systematic traders isn't a weak language. It's never finishing anything.

sections.heading: Pine Script Is Deliberately Crippled, and That Is the Point
sections.content:
Pine is a domain-specific language with a series execution model. Your script runs once per bar, left to right, and every variable is really a time series you're indexing into. There's no file system, no network calls, no package manager, no environment. You get data, drawing objects and a strategy tester, and TradingView handles the rest. The official Pine Script documentation is one of the few language references I'd tell someone to read start to finish, because it's short enough to actually finish.

The limits are real and they're published. Loops that chew more than roughly half a second on a single bar get killed. You're capped on request.security calls, on labels, lines and boxes, and on how far back a script can look without you declaring it. You cannot rank 500 symbols against each other, and you cannot run a portfolio-level backtest with shared capital across instruments. Those aren't bugs. They're the price of running your code on someone else's servers for free.

Here's the part developers underrate: constraints force you to express the idea instead of the infrastructure. I've watched engineers with fifteen years of shipping experience produce nothing tradeable for six months because Python let them build a framework. Pine won't let you. You get an entry condition, an exit condition and a chart that shows you were wrong, usually within the hour.

sections.heading: What Python Costs You Before Your First Honest Backtest
sections.content:
Python is the correct long-term answer, and I say that as someone who now runs everything live in it. Python turned up in about 51 percent of responses in the 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, which matters here for a boring reason. Popularity means libraries, and libraries mean you're not the person implementing a Kalman filter or an exchange websocket reconnect loop from scratch.

But price the setup honestly. Before your first backtest you need clean historical data, a survivorship-bias-free universe if you're doing equities, a corporate actions story, a backtest engine you trust, and a broker connection. Every one of those is a project. The broker layer in particular moves under you. Anyone who built on ib_insync for Interactive Brokers found the project archived in 2024 after its author passed away, and the community migrated to the ib_async fork. That's maintenance work Pine users simply never do.

So the tradeoff is not power versus simplicity. It's time-to-first-wrong-answer. Pine gets you wrong fast. Python gets you wrong slowly and expensively, and if you're still learning what a decent edge looks like, fast is worth more. There's a longer version of this argument in the case that the Pine versus Python answer isn't obvious, and I mostly agree with it.

sections.heading: The One Question That Decides It
sections.content:
Ask yourself this: do you already have a strategy you believe in, written down as rules, that Pine cannot express? If the honest answer is no, open Pine. If the answer is yes, and you can name the specific blocker, open Python. That's the whole decision rule, and I've used it with maybe thirty people now.

The blockers that genuinely justify Python from day one are narrow:

  • Cross-sectional work, like ranking a universe and holding the top decile
  • Anything needing options chains, order book depth or tick-level fills
  • Machine learning beyond a hand-rolled regression
  • Execution against a broker Pine's alerts can't reach reliably
  • Portfolio construction with shared capital and real position sizing

Everything else, and I mean nearly everything a discretionary trader wants to systematize, fits in Pine. Momentum filters, volatility regimes, session logic, multi-timeframe confirmation, trailing exits. In my work with retail traders moving into automation, more than half never hit a blocker at all. They hit boredom, or they hit the discovery that their idea didn't work, which is a much cheaper lesson at forty minutes than at eleven days.

sections.heading: Where Pine Runs Out of Road, and the Trap Waiting in Python
sections.content:
Pine's strategy tester lies to you in specific, learnable ways. Default order sizing is one contract unless you change it. Intrabar fills are approximated unless you're on a plan with deep backtesting and bar magnifier, which sits on the Premium tier at somewhere around $50 to $60 a month depending on how you bill it. Repainting from careless request.security calls will hand you a beautiful curve that evaporates live. None of that is unique to Pine, though. The gap between test and reality is structural, and I wrote about why backtest and live results always diverge for anyone who wants the mechanics.

My friend Dev tried to skip Pine entirely and honestly... it went badly? He's a stronger engineer than I am. He spent about three weekends building a genuinely lovely event-driven backtester with a proper matching engine, and then never traded a single strategy with it because he kept refactoring the config loader. I did the same thing in a different flavour in 2022, wrote an elegant abstract BaseStrategy class that had exactly one subclass for the rest of its life. I'm not sure this happens to everyone. But if you enjoy building tools more than you enjoy being publicly wrong about markets, Python will let you hide in the tooling for months and call it progress.

The other trap is statistical, and it's the reason I'm suspicious of people who jump straight to Python for the optimization power. Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu showed in Notices of the AMS (2014) that with only two years of daily data, roughly seven independent trials are enough to produce an in-sample Sharpe of 1.0 whose expected out-of-sample Sharpe is zero. Python makes running ten thousand trials trivial. Pine makes it annoying. Being slow at overfitting is an underrated advantage. The counterargument is fair: Pine's friction also stops you from doing proper walk-forward validation, so you trade one bias for another. That debate is genuinely open.

article.conclusion: Do this today. Open a chart, hit Pine Editor, and rewrite one rule you already trade by hand into a strategy() script with real position sizing and a commission setting. Ninety minutes, not ninety days. When you hit the first thing Pine won't let you do, write that blocker down in a file, and when the file has three entries, that's your signal to start on Python. The path from one to the other is covered in learn Pine first and switch when it hurts, and the hurting is the part you should wait for.

faq.q: Can I automate real trades with Pine Script alone?
faq.a: Only indirectly. Pine sends alerts, and you need a webhook receiver plus a broker API to turn those alerts into orders, which means you end up writing Python anyway. Native broker execution inside TradingView is limited to the brokers it integrates with, and fill behaviour differs from the strategy tester.

faq.q: How long does Pine Script take to learn if I already code?
faq.a: A weekend for the syntax, about two weeks to stop fighting the bar-by-bar series model. The series semantics are the only genuinely unfamiliar part for someone coming from an imperative background, because every variable is a time series and history access uses the square bracket operator.

faq.q: Is Pine Script code portable to Python later?
faq.a: The logic is, the structure isn't. You'll rewrite rather than translate, since Pine's implicit per-bar loop becomes an explicit loop or a vectorized pandas operation. Budget a day per non-trivial strategy, and expect the results to differ until you match commission, slippage and fill timing exactly.

topic: How professional trading desks evaluate new tools

article.title: Trading Desks Kill Most New Tools in 20 Minutes
article.meta_description: How professional trading desks evaluate new tools, from the FIX failure questions vendors dodge to the integration costs nobody puts in the quote.
article.author: Alex Turner
article.intro: Professional desks don't evaluate tools by feature list. They try to break them, usually inside the first twenty minutes, and every question is about failure modes rather than functionality. I sat in on an execution management system demo in March 2024 where the head of trading asked exactly one thing before anything else: what happens to working orders when your FIX session drops mid-fill? The sales engineer said he'd follow up by email. Call ended at eleven minutes, and nobody on our side felt bad about it. That's the real evaluation process, compressed, and it's the opposite of how almost every vendor prepares.
article.intro2: The reason desks are this blunt is arithmetic. The BIS Triennial Central Bank Survey put global FX turnover at roughly $7.5 trillion per day in April 2022, and a tool sitting in that flow doesn't get to have an interesting bug. A broken chart is annoying. A broken order state machine is a P&L event with a compliance report attached. So the buying process reverses: instead of proving what it does, the tool has to prove what it does when things go wrong.

sections.heading: The First Twenty Minutes Are a Deliberate Ambush
sections.content:
Every desk I've worked with has an informal kill list. Nobody writes it down, but it's stable across firms, and it's aimed squarely at the parts of a product that demos never show. The point isn't to be difficult. It's to find out fast whether the vendor has ever run this thing under stress.

The questions look roughly like this:

  • What's your behaviour on session disconnect with live working orders, and who owns reconciliation afterwards?
  • Show me the audit trail for a cancel-replace that got rejected by the venue.
  • What's your p99 latency, measured where, and can I see the histogram rather than the average?
  • What happens at 10x normal message volume, and have you actually tested that or are you extrapolating?
  • Who else on the street runs this in production, and can I talk to their tech lead, not their salesperson?

Averages are the tell. When a vendor quotes mean latency, they're either hiding the tail or they never instrumented it, and in my experience it's usually the second one. I've watched a market data adapter benchmark at 400 microseconds average and then blow out past 40 milliseconds during a CPI print, which is precisely the moment you cared. The mean was honest. The mean was also useless. I've dug into the pattern of vendors failing this exact test before in a longer piece on why most vendors fail the desk's first test, and the failure is remarkably consistent.

sections.heading: The Integration Tax Is the Real Price Tag
sections.content:
Here's my strongest opinion on this, and it puts me at odds with most procurement people: license cost is close to irrelevant compared with integration cost, and desks that optimise on price get burned about eighteen months later. A $60,000 a year platform that eats four months of a senior developer's time is more expensive than a $180,000 one that ships a clean REST and FIX interface with real sandbox credentials.

What developers actually check

When I'm the one doing technical due diligence, I ignore the deck entirely and go straight for the API docs. Are the error responses documented with actual codes, or is there a shrug paragraph about "contact support"? Is there a sandbox I can hit today without a signed NDA? Does the SDK pin its dependencies? Is there a changelog, and does it show breaking changes being handled with versioned endpoints rather than a Friday afternoon surprise?

One thing I look for that sounds petty but predicts everything: timestamp precision and timezone handling. If a vendor's API returns local time without an offset, or truncates to seconds on a fills feed, that tells you the engineering culture in about ninety seconds. You've just learned something no reference call would have given you. The same instinct applies when you're assessing free alternatives, which is partly why I keep coming back to which open-source trading bots are actually worth running rather than assuming paid means safer.

sections.heading: Paper Trading Proves Almost Nothing
sections.content:
Desks that know what they're doing insist on a live capital pilot, usually small and usually boring. Somewhere between $10,000 and $50,000 of real risk, run for four to six weeks in a strategy nobody cares much about. The reason is simple. Simulated fills are a fiction the vendor controls, and a paper engine will happily fill you at the mid on a size that would have moved the book.

I'll admit I'm less certain here than I sound... my friend Priya runs a small options book in Chicago and she skipped the live pilot on a risk engine last year because the vendor had two tier-one banks as references, and it worked out completely fine for her. Meanwhile I did the careful thing on a different product, ran the pilot properly, and still missed a rounding bug in the position aggregator that only appeared on partial fills of odd lots. Found it three months later. On a Tuesday. I'd spent the whole pilot watching latency graphs like a hawk and never once summed the positions by hand, which in retrospect is a genuinely embarrassing thing for someone who writes about this to admit. So pilots catch a lot, but they catch what you thought to look for, and not much else.

The gap between simulated and live behaviour deserves its own treatment, and I've written about why backtest results and live fills drift apart in detail. Every argument in that piece applies to tool evaluation too.

sections.heading: Vendor Risk Now Comes With a Regulator Attached
sections.content:
The compliance layer has stopped being paperwork. Under SEC Rule 15c3-5, adopted in 2010, broker-dealers providing market access have to own their pre-trade risk controls directly. You can't outsource that judgement to a vendor's black box, which kills any product that won't explain its risk check logic in plain terms.

In Europe it got sharper. The Digital Operational Resilience Act has applied since 17 January 2025, and ESMA now expects firms to maintain a register of ICT third-party providers, contractual exit strategies, and evidence of resilience testing. In practice that means a new tool needs a documented plan for how you'd rip it out before it goes in.

There's real debate about whether this helps. The critique I hear most, and I have some sympathy with it, is that heavy vendor governance quietly favours the incumbents who can afford the compliance staff, which slows down the smaller shops building genuinely better technology. That's a fair worry. It's also not an argument for skipping the exit plan.

article.conclusion: Do this today: open the API documentation of whatever tool you're currently considering and find the error code reference. If there isn't one, or it's a support email address, stop the evaluation there and save yourself the demo. That single check has killed more bad tools for me than any structured scorecard ever did.

faq.q: How long does a trading desk trial usually last?
faq.a: Four to six weeks with live capital is the common range, often $10,000 to $50,000 of real risk in a low-priority strategy. Anything shorter rarely covers a volatile session, and anything longer tends to mean the decision has already stalled internally.

faq.q: Should I test a trading tool in paper mode first?
faq.a: Use paper mode only to verify wiring and message formats. Fill quality, slippage behaviour and position reconciliation are the things that actually differ, and none of them show up until real orders hit a real venue.

faq.q: What makes a vendor fail technical due diligence fastest?
faq.a: Quoting average latency instead of tail percentiles, and shipping API docs with no documented error codes. Both signal that nobody instrumented the product properly, which almost always predicts problems during high message volume.

topic: How to paper trade before risking real capital

article.title: Your Paper Trading Account Is Lying About Your Fills
article.meta_description: Paper trade the right way: model fills, fees and latency, run one code path in sim and live, and track the six numbers that predict survival.
article.author: Alex Turner
article.intro: Paper trade for at least 60 sessions, and log every simulated fill against the order book you would actually have hit. That second part is what almost nobody does. In March 2023 I ran a mean reversion strategy on ETH perps inside a broker sim for six weeks, printed a 31% paper return, and went live with $8,000 on a Tuesday morning. Eleven days later I was down about $1,400, and the signal was fine. The simulator had been filling me at the mid price on every entry, and my real orders were crossing a 4 basis point spread and paying taker fees on top.
article.intro2: So my position is blunt. Paper trading is worth your time, but only if you treat the simulator as software under test rather than as an oracle. Most retail platforms ship a sim that's built to make you feel good enough to fund the account. The fill engine is optimistic, the fee schedule is often ignored, and latency is zero. You're testing your idea against a market that doesn't exist.

sections.heading: Every Paper Fill You Get Is a Story the Broker Made Up
sections.content:
Open your sim's docs and find the fill logic. Usually you can't, because there isn't any documented. What you typically get: market orders filled at the last traded price, limit orders filled the instant price touches your level, unlimited size, no partial fills, and no funding or borrow cost. Four separate flattering assumptions stacked on one equity curve.

Write your own fill model, even a crude one. Mine is maybe 40 lines. Market orders walk the book from the best offer and pay the taker fee. Limit orders only fill once price trades through my level by at least one tick, on the theory that I'm last in the queue, which I usually am. Every order gets delayed by the round trip time I measured against the exchange, which for me was around 90ms on a Frankfurt box. That single change took my ETH backtest from 31% to roughly 6%. Painful, and correct. If you want to model queue position properly rather than guess, you need book updates rather than snapshots, which is the whole argument for treating market microstructure as a stream processing problem.

The misconception I see constantly is that paper trading exists to prove a strategy is profitable. It doesn't. It proves your plumbing works and gives you a pessimistic floor on performance. Profitability gets decided by live money.

sections.heading: One Code Path, Two Adapters, No Exceptions
sections.content:
If your paper loop is a notebook and your live loop is a daemon, you tested nothing. You tested a different program. I've seen this pattern in almost every codebase I've reviewed for other traders, and it's where the ugly surprises hide: a timezone difference in the notebook, a rounding rule for tick size that only exists in the live path, a reconnect handler that never ran in sim because the sim never disconnects.

Structure it so the strategy module imports an interface with the same methods, and you swap the implementation behind a config flag. Same event loop, same state machine, same logging, same position tracker. The only thing that changes is whether submit_order talks to the exchange or to your fill model. Do the same for data: if you're going to run live off a socket, run your paper mode off that identical socket rather than polled snapshots, because the gap between WebSocket streams and REST polling shows up as phantom signals your live system will never see.

sections.heading: Six Numbers That Predict Whether You Survive
sections.content:
Return percentage is close to useless at this stage. Track these instead, per session, in a real table you can query:

  • Fill count. Under 200 fills you have an anecdote, not a sample.
  • Realized slippage versus modeled slippage, in basis points per trade.
  • Fee and funding drag as a share of gross P&L. Anything over 30% and your edge belongs to the exchange.
  • Maximum adverse excursion on winning trades, which tells you if your stops are about to get eaten.
  • Worst rolling 5 day drawdown, not the total drawdown.
  • Time to recovery after that drawdown.

Sample size matters more than people accept. A study of Brazilian futures day traders published by Chague, De-Losso and Giovannetti found that among those who persisted beyond 300 days, roughly 97% lost money, and only about 1.1% earned more than the Brazilian minimum wage (Day Trading for a Living?). The retail picture in Europe is similar. When ESMA restricted CFDs, it cited national regulator data showing between 74% and 89% of retail accounts lost money (ESMA). Six good weeks in a simulator doesn't move you out of those distributions.

Okay, slight tangent, but my friend Dev pushed back hard on all of this last summer and I don't think he was entirely wrong. He skipped the sim completely and just traded 0.01 lots for three months, said the fake money made him sloppy. And honestly... I sort of envy how quickly he learned to size down. I did the opposite once, in 2022, and got so attached to a paper account showing $2.3M that I actually screenshotted it and sent it to my brother. Real balance at the time was $11,000. I'm not 100% sure the sim-first path is right for everybody. It's right for anyone shipping code, because code has bugs and bugs cost more than pride.

sections.heading: Where the Simulator Runs Out of Road
sections.content:
Two things paper trading cannot give you, and pretending otherwise is how people blow up. The first is your own behavior under loss. No simulator reproduces the specific nausea of watching real rent money drop 8% in nine minutes, and that feeling is what makes people widen stops and double down. The second is market impact. If your live size is meaningful relative to displayed depth, your own orders move the price, and no sim accounts for the liquidity you consume.

My answer is to run both in parallel rather than treating them as stages. Keep the sim running permanently as a correctness harness, because that's what catches the reconnect bug and the off-by-one in your position sizing. Then go live with the smallest size the venue allows, something where a total loss costs you a decent dinner, and run it alongside. When the live fills and the modeled fills agree within a couple of basis points across 200 trades, your simulator has earned the right to be believed. Not before.

article.conclusion: Do this today: add a second equity curve to your logs. For every simulated trade, record an optimistic fill at mid price and a pessimistic fill that crosses the full spread, pays the taker fee, and assumes a 100ms delay. Plot both. Trade only what the pessimistic curve says you have, and if that curve is flat, you found out for free.

faq.q: How long should I paper trade before going live?
faq.a: Count fills, not weeks. Aim for at least 200 simulated fills across varied conditions, which for most intraday systems lands somewhere around 8 to 12 weeks. If your strategy trades twice a month, you need a longer historical replay instead.

faq.q: Does paper trading actually work, or is it a waste of time?
faq.a: It works for testing your code, your data feed, your order routing and your risk limits. It fails at testing your emotional response and your market impact. Use it to remove bugs, then use tiny real size to test yourself.

faq.q: Which paper trading platform gives the most realistic fills?
faq.a: Interactive Brokers and Tradovate are closer to reality than most retail crypto sims, but none of them model queue position properly. The most realistic option is your own fill model running against recorded order book data from the venue you plan to trade.
